title: DNAME Redirection in the DNS
summary: The DNAME record redirects a whole subtree of the DNS: every name ending in a given suffix is mapped to the same part of another tree. It obsoletes RFC 2672 and updates RFC 3363.

eli5.summary: If a street gets a new name, a sign sends everything on the old street to the new one, not one house at a time.

questions: what is a dns dname record
subtitle: A DNS record that redirects a whole subtree of names to another part of the name tree.

tldr.problem: A CNAME can alias only a single name, so there is no way to point every name under a domain at the matching names under another domain.
tldr.mechanism: The DNAME record replaces the suffix of any name below its owner with its target name, and servers synthesize a CNAME so that clients that do not know DNAME still work.
tldr.outcome: This revision of RFC 2672 changes no wire format. It clarifies substitution rules, fixes the synthesized CNAME TTL, and adds guidance on DNSSEC, dynamic update and wildcards.

facts.label: RDATA
facts.value: One field, the target name, sent uncompressed

facts.label: Per name
facts.value: One DNAME; no CNAME at the same name

today: RFC 6672 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2012. It obsoletes RFC 2672 and updates RFC 3363. No later RFC obsoletes it.

sections.title: What DNAME Does
sections.content:
The DNAME resource record redirects part of the DNS name tree to another part. A CNAME sends a lookup for its own owner name to one other name. A DNAME instead directs lookups for data at the descendants of its owner's name to corresponding names under a different node of the tree.

For example, if a DNAME at example.com points to example.net, a query for foo.example.com becomes a query for foo.example.net, and www.foo.example.com becomes www.foo.example.net.

The RFC gives two uses. DNAME was conceived to help maintain address-to-name mappings when a network is renumbered, as in classless reverse delegations. It can also alias name spaces so that subtrees hold the same information, for instance punycode alternates for domain spaces. This revision of RFC 2672 does not change the wire format or the handling of DNAME records; it adds discussion of problems that may arise.
sections.eli5: A CNAME is a sign saying one house moved. A DNAME is a sign saying everything on this street moved to another street, with the house numbers staying the same.

sections.title: The DNAME Record and Substitution
sections.content:
The DNAME record has type code 39 and is CLASS-insensitive. Its data is a single field, <target>, a fully qualified domain name that MUST be sent uncompressed and MUST be present. The owner name can be compressed like any other, and the target MUST be downcased for DNSSEC validation.

A DNAME substitution replaces the suffix labels of the name being sought that match the DNAME's owner name with the target. Only whole labels are replaced, so ab.example.com. does not match a DNAME owned by b.example.com.. The substitution applies at every DNAME found along the way, so valid chains can be fairly long. DNAMEs and CNAMEs can form loops, so resolvers and servers should be cautious about the resources they spend, and zone administrators should avoid loops.

If substitution makes the name too long, the server returns RCODE YXDOMAIN (value 6) and includes the DNAME record and its signature as proof. The RFC's example is a 250-octet target with a first label over 5 octets, which gives a name over 255 octets.

Unlike a CNAME, a DNAME does not redirect its own owner name. The owner may hold other record types, except DNAME, CNAME or types that cannot coexist with them. A query that matches one of those types is answered from the owner name, not the target. DNAME MUST NOT share an owner name with an NS record unless that name is the zone apex. A DNAME at the apex does not mirror the apex, so the usual SOA and NS records are still needed.
sections.eli5: The sign only changes the front part of the address, the street. Names must match whole words, and if the new address gets too long to write down, the answer is an error.

sections.title: How Servers and Resolvers Process It
sections.content:
When a server applies a DNAME it includes the DNAME record in the answer section and also synthesizes a CNAME for the query name, with the same TTL as the DNAME. The owner of that CNAME is the QNAME. DNSSEC says the synthesized CNAME need not be signed, because a validating resolver can check it against the signed DNAME. Servers MUST be able to answer a query for a synthesized CNAME. A cache SHOULD give the CNAME the decremented TTL of the cached DNAME. Resolvers MUST accept a synthesized CNAME TTL of zero or equal to the DNAME's, since some older servers used zero.

The RFC gives revised server and resolver algorithms. In the server algorithm, when a label has no match, the server checks whether the last matched label has a DNAME. If so it copies the record into the answer, sets YXDOMAIN if the substitution would overflow, otherwise substitutes, MUST synthesize the CNAME and starts over. Recursive caching servers MUST perform CNAME synthesis on behalf of clients.

Data may briefly exist below a DNAME in a cache after a change. Caches can keep both versions, or drop the old data or the longer name, and consistency returns when the older TTL expires. A DNSSEC-validated DNAME that contradicts the cache SHOULD be cached; an unvalidated one SHOULD NOT.

Wildcard DNAMEs such as *.example.com DNAME example.net SHOULD NOT be used. Processing is non-deterministic, so DNSSEC validators may be unable to validate them.
sections.eli5: A server that knows about the sign also writes a note saying exactly where this one name goes, so even a helper who never learned about street signs can follow along.

sections.title: Other Constraints and Dynamic Update
sections.content:
Records MUST NOT exist at any subdomain of a DNAME's owner. A server MAY refuse to load a zone with such data; if it loads one, the names below the DNAME are occluded. DNAME is a singleton type: one DNAME per name, and no CNAME at that name.

Names listed as targets of MX, NS, PTR and SRV records must be canonical hostnames, so they cannot fall under a DNAME. The RFC's example is a zone with punycode alternates using DNAME, where the MX, NS, SRV and PTR data must carry the already-substituted names.

With dynamic update, adding a DNAME to a zone occludes any names below it. If a CNAME already exists at that owner name, the new DNAME MUST be ignored. If a DNAME exists, the new one replaces it. Likewise, a CNAME added where a DNAME exists MUST be ignored.

The RFC also revises RFC 3363. That document deprecated DNAME in the IPv6 reverse tree, and this one drops the constraints on having DNAME records in those zones.
sections.eli5: Only one sign can stand on a street, and nobody may put houses under it, because the sign already says where the street goes.

sections.title: DNSSEC and DNAME
sections.content:
A signed DNAME means a non-terminal redirection. The synthesized CNAME, if present, is never signed, so a validator checks the DNAME and then that the CNAME was properly synthesized.

In negative responses, the NSEC or NSEC3 type bitmap SHOULD be checked for a DNAME that should have been applied. In the RFC's example, an NXDOMAIN for foo.bar.example.com backed by an NSEC for bar.example.com with the DNAME bit set is bogus, because the name should have been redirected. For cee.example.com the same NSEC is valid, since that name is not redirected.

A chain of DNAME and CNAME redirections is only as strong as its weakest link: the AD (Authentic Data) bit can be set only if every step is secure, and one bogus step makes the result bogus. Validating resolvers MUST understand DNAME. The unsigned synthesized CNAME cannot be trusted by itself, so the validator verifies the DNAME signature and resolves the target name itself.
sections.eli5: The signed sign is trustworthy, but the helper's note is not signed. So a careful checker trusts the sign and works out the new address on their own.

sections.title: Examples of Use
sections.content:
Organizational renaming. If frobozz.example.net joins acme.example.com, its old zone can carry a DNAME pointing to frobozz-division.acme.example.com. The MX record at the apex is not redirected and must be repeated in the target zone.

Classless reverse delegation. The scheme of RFC 2317 can be extended to prefixes shorter than 24 bits with DNAME. The RFC shows 192.0.8.0/22 delegated with an NS record and four DNAME records for 8, 9, 10 and 11.

Renumbering. Using DNAME rather than NS records to delegate could simplify maintenance if IPv4 renumbering were common. The RFC notes the value may be low because renumbering involves far more than the DNS, but hopes DNAME may help in IPv6.
sections.eli5: If a company merges with another, a sign at the old address sends all visitors to the new building, and the same trick helps when a whole block of addresses is renumbered.
